summary: Specifies a Neighbor Discovery option for Router Advertisements that tells hosts the IPv6 prefix used for NAT64, which translates from IPv6 clients to IPv4 servers.

eli5.summary: A router posts a sign telling devices which doorway to use to reach old-style addresses.

questions: how do hosts discover the nat64 prefix
what is the pref64 option format
subtitle: A Router Advertisement option that tells IPv6-only hosts which prefix reaches IPv4 through NAT64.

tldr.problem: Hosts on IPv6-only networks that use NAT64 often need to know the NAT64 prefix, for example to synthesize addresses or to translate IPv4 literals, but had no way to learn it from the same message that configures the rest of their network.
tldr.mechanism: A new Neighbor Discovery option, the PREF64 option (type 38), carries the NAT64 prefix, its length code and a scaled lifetime inside the Router Advertisements that routers already send.
tldr.outcome: Hosts learn the prefix in the one packet that configures the rest of the network, and routers can change it later by sending a new RA.

today: RFC 8781 is a Proposed Standard from April 2020. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why Hosts Need the NAT64 Prefix
sections.content:
NAT64 with DNS64 lets hosts on an IPv6-only network reach IPv4 servers. The RFC calls it a widely deployed mechanism. In several situations the host itself must know the NAT64 prefix (called PREF64) that the network uses.

RFC 8781 defines a Neighbor Discovery option, carried in Router Advertisements (RAs), that communicates NAT64 prefixes to hosts.
sections.eli5: Some devices need to know the secret doorway to the old internet. This document says the router should just tell them.

sections.title: Use Cases and Why Use RAs
sections.content:
The RFC lists two groups of uses. For DNS64 on the host: local DNSSEC validation with a stub resolver, using a trusted DNS server that the network does not provide (such as DNS-over-TLS or DNS-over-HTTPS), and networks with no DNS64 server at all. For address translation on the host: translating IPv4 address literals on an IPv6-only host, and 464XLAT.

It then gives four reasons to put the prefix in RAs. Fate sharing: NAT64 needs routing, and IPv6 routing configuration needs an RA. Atomic configuration: one packet completes configuration, so a host never has an incomplete Layer 3 setup. Updatability: a new RA can announce a changed prefix. Deployability: all IPv6 hosts already support Neighbor Discovery, so only a small extension is needed, unlike options such as PCP that need another protocol.
sections.eli5: The router already tells every new device how to get online. Adding the doorway to that same message means nothing gets missed and the sign is easy to change.

sections.title: The PREF64 Option Format
sections.content:
The option has a Type of 38, a Length, a 13-bit Scaled Lifetime, a 3-bit Prefix Length Code (PLC) and the highest 96 bits of the prefix. Length is in units of 8 octets, and the sender MUST set it to 2. The receiver MUST ignore the option if Length is not 2.

The PLC values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 mean prefix lengths of 96, 64, 56, 48, 40 and 32 bits. A receiver MUST ignore the option if the PLC is any other value.
sections.eli5: The sign has a fixed size. It has a number for how long the doorway address is, a timer for how long the sign is good for, and the address itself.

sections.title: Scaled Lifetime
sections.content:
The lifetime is counted in units of 8 seconds, so the receiver MUST multiply the field by 8 to get seconds. The longest possible lifetime is therefore 65528 seconds. Because of this, it is NOT RECOMMENDED to configure default Router Lifetimes greater than 65528 seconds when using this option. A lifetime of 0 means the prefix SHOULD NOT be used anymore.

By default the field SHOULD be set to the lesser of 3 x MaxRtrAdvInterval divided by 8, or 8191. Router vendors SHOULD let administrators enter nonzero lifetimes that are not divisible by 8; the router SHOULD round up to the next multiple of 8 and divide by 8. If a nonzero value is less than 8, the field SHOULD be set to 1 so it stays nonzero.
sections.eli5: The timer counts in chunks of 8 seconds so it fits in a small space. A timer of zero means the sign is taken down.

sections.title: Usage Guidelines
sections.content:
One option names exactly one NAT64 prefix for all IPv4 destinations. An operator who wants different parts of IPv4 to go to different NAT64 devices can route more specific subprefixes of the NAT64 prefix to those devices. The RFC's example sends 2001:db8:a:b::a00:0/104 to one device and 2001:db8:a:b::/96 to another.

The option may appear more than once in an RA, for instance while renumbering from one prefix to another. Hosts SHOULD follow Section 3 of RFC 7050, limited to prefixes with a nonzero lifetime. If a host finds prefixes by several mechanisms, it SHOULD pick one source only, in this recommended order: PCP-discovered, then the RA option, then the RFC 7050 method. The host SHOULD treat the prefix as specific to the interface it arrived on, and hosts aware of Provisioning Domains MUST scope it to the right one.

The option cannot tell hosts that certain IPv4 ranges should not be translated, a limit it shares with other provisioning mechanisms.
sections.eli5: If there are several signs, a device follows a fixed order of which one to trust. Each sign only counts for the hallway where it was seen.

sections.title: Consistency Checks Between Routers
sections.content: Routers SHOULD inspect valid PREF64 options sent by other routers on the same link and check that they agree. They compare the set of PREF64s with a nonzero lifetime and the set with a zero lifetime. A mismatch suggests a router is misconfigured, and routers SHOULD log it to system or network management. Routers aware of Provisioning Domains MUST only compare information in the same domain.
sections.eli5: Routers on the same street check that their signs match, and tell the boss if they do not.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
RAs are needed on IPv6-only networks anyway, so they must already be protected, for example with RA-Guard. Putting more configuration in RAs gives attackers fewer mechanisms to target. A wrong prefix could stop a host reaching IPv4-only destinations but would not affect IPv6 destinations. Attackers who can send rogue RAs can still mount denial-of-service or man-in-the-middle attacks.

IANA assigned type 38 to the PREF64 option in the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Option Formats registry.
sections.eli5: A fake sign could send you to the wrong doorway, so routers must already guard against fakes.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Option length in units of 8 octets.

fields.name: Scaled Lifetime
fields.desc: Maximum time in units of 8 seconds the prefix may be used.

fields.name: Highest 96 bits of the Prefix
fields.desc: Bits 0 to 95 of the NAT64 prefix.
